newsitem.title: UK: London cocoa jumps to 10-week high, weather worries.
newsitem.headline: London cocoa jumps to 10-week high, weather worries.

text.p: London cocoa futures climbed amid heavy turnover to a 10-week high on Thursday on worries that developing weather patterns could affect next year's crops.

The July contract opened strongly, about 10 pounds sterling above Wednesday's best, and never looked back. It was up 37 stg at 1,062 stg per tonne, the highest since April 4, at Thursday's midsession,
Once July got through key resistance levels and September broke 1,072, fresh technical buying from funds carried prices even higher, traders said.
Traders saw the catalyst for the buying spree in fears that the developing "El Nino" weather pattern could produce damaging dry weather in key cocoa producing countries.

El Nino can affect global weather patterns for up to 18 months, depending on how soon ocean temperatures return to normal. The last major El Nino lasted from late 1991 to mid-1992. A less severe one was seen from 1994 to 1995.

On Tuesday, the U.S. National Oceanic and Atmospheric Administration (NOAA) said warm ocean temperatures off the western coast of South America had triggered an El Nino weather pattern that could have an impact on crops around the world, including West Africa, the largest cocoa producing region.

Larry Acker, analyst at 3F Forecasts in Polo, Ill., said in his May 5 newsletter that he expected El Nino by September, marked by a shift of drought and flooding patterns starting no later than August.
He expected unstable and dry weather in West Africa in coming months, which may continue to boost cocoa prices.
Speculation has already surfaced that Ivory Coast cocoa settings for the new crop have remained low, traders said.
Southeast Asia, including number three cocoa producer Indonesia, is also closely watching for possible drought due to El Nino.

"I will be keeping a close eye on production levels in June and July to see if there has been any impact, a senior Indonesian cocoa industry official said on Thursday. "It is already getting difficult to get cocoa beans now."
El Nino-related drought fears first spurred speculators to buy back short positions set last week when cocoa prices looked posied for a new downturn, traders said.

That initial buying bolstered July to close strongly for three consecutive days and pushed the contract through significant, triple resistance levels between 1,040 and 1,060 to turn a sideways-moving technicals chart into a more bullish picture and attract fresh buying.

Trevor Neil, senior technical analyst at Union Cal Futures, said July break out of a flag formation on daily charts amid heavy turnover of 12,728 contracts this morning could mean a move toward 1,160.
Origins were mostly quiet amid the buying spree, traders said.
When New York opens, traders expected a quick wave of arbitrage to close the gap between the two markets resulting from London's steep climb this morning.
In options, only puts traded. Twenty-five September 1,000 and 50 September 1,025 puts changed hands.
